title: Sabzi polo
subtitle: Persian herb rice with dill, parsley, and coriander
excerpt: Sabzi polo is Persian herb rice: basmati cooked using the chelow method with large quantities of fresh dill, parsley, and coriander folded through the grains. The herbs turn vivid green in the steam and perfume the whole pot. It is traditionally served with fish at the Persian New Year.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Sabzi polo mahi is the centrepiece of the Nowruz table, described in detail. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Herb mixture and proportions documented.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The herbs can be chopped up to two hours ahead. The rice is best made fresh and served immediately.

content.text: Sabzi polo is Persian herb rice, made using the same two-stage chelow method as plain steamed rice but with large amounts of fresh dill, parsley, and coriander folded through the grains before steaming. The herbs cook gently in the steam and turn from bright to a deeper green while keeping their flavour. The tahdig at the base is flecked with herb. Serve alongside grilled or baked fish, or with khoresh.

items.prepNote: rinsed three times until the water runs clear

content.text: Bring a large pot of water to the boil and add {{sea-salt-fine}}. Add the rinsed {{basmati-rice}} and parboil for six to seven minutes until tender outside but still chalky in the centre. Drain well in a colander.
Toss the drained rice with {{dill}}, {{parsley-flat}}, {{coriander}}, and {{spring-onion}} if using. Mix gently so the herbs are well distributed.
Heat {{sunflower-oil}} and 3 tablespoons of water in a large heavy saucepan over medium-high heat. When hot, spread a thin layer of the herb rice over the base, pressing gently.

Mound the remaining herb rice on top. Wrap the lid in a clean tea towel and place firmly on the pan. Cook on medium-high for three minutes to build steam, then reduce to the lowest possible heat and steam for 30 to 35 minutes.

Remove from the heat and place the pan on a cold wet cloth for two minutes. Spoon the fluffy herb rice onto a platter, then invert the pan to release the herb-flecked tahdig crust. Add {{unsalted-butter}} over the hot rice to melt if using.

items.symptom: The herbs turn grey and taste bitter
items.cause: Heat too high during steaming or cooked for too long
items.fix: The steaming phase must be at the lowest heat. Thirty to thirty-five minutes is enough. Overheating overcooks the herbs.

items.symptom: The tahdig burns at the base
items.cause: Heat not reduced quickly enough after the initial steam build
items.fix: Drop to the lowest setting immediately after three minutes on medium-high. A heat diffuser helps with electric hobs.

items.symptom: The rice tastes bland despite all the herbs
items.fix: The parboiling water should taste noticeably salty, like pasta water. Salt added at this stage penetrates the grain.

items.symptom: The herbs sink to the bottom rather than distributing evenly
items.cause: Mixed in too forcefully, breaking the rice grains
items.fix: Toss gently with two forks. The herbs should coat the grains without being squashed into them.

content.text: Sabzi polo mahi (herb rice with fish) is the traditional Nowruz meal eaten on the Persian New Year, which falls at the spring equinox in late March. The herbs represent the new growth of spring, and the fish (usually white fish or salmon) represents life and fertility. The combination is eaten at the first meal of the year across Iran and the Iranian diaspora worldwide. Outside the New Year context, sabzi polo is also a standard accompaniment to grilled or braised fish throughout the year. The herb mix varies: some families use dried herbs in winter when fresh are unavailable, though the flavour is noticeably less vibrant.
